title: Cyber Resilient Weapon Systems Body of Knowledge Portal 3.23.22

cues.text: >> I'd like to thank everyone for joining today's DAU web event.
Today, we have the Cyber Resilient Weapon Systems Body of Knowledge Portal.
My name is Emmett Simmons.
I'm the producer for today's event.
We also have Aaron Jacobson on as our host.
The agenda for today is posted.
Your microphones will be muted throughout the session.
The session is being recorded.
It will be posted to dau.edu/events.
Please submit all your questions via the chat.
We'll respond to your questions towards the end of the event.
There is a survey at the end where we will post a link to the survey in the chat.
It takes a couple minutes to fill it out.
We appreciate you for it.
If you're here for CLPs, this session does qualify for one CLP with supervisor approval.
It is not automatic.
You will have to apply for it.
At the end of the survey, there's a section to put your e mail address in,
and it will e mail you a CLP certificate to submit if you need it.
And now I'm going to turn it over to Aaron to introduce our speakers.
>> All right.
Thank you, Emmett.
Good morning, everybody.
Aaron Jacobson here, professor of cybersecurity at DAU, learning asset manager for SCRE,
which is secure cyber resilient engineering.
Today, we're going to visit cyber resilient weapon system body of knowledge portal.
The body of knowledge provides a comprehensive repository of publicly available guidance
and knowledge to assist a workforce in the engineering of cyber resilient weapon systems.
Users can include engineering, engineer and science technology manager with research,
researchers from across DoD, federal government industry and academia, can now access
and share crucial engineering information needed to develop, maintain,
and monitor secure cyber resilient weapon system programs.
First, I'm going to introduce Ms. Angela Lungu.
She provides support to the resilient system policy guidance and standards for OUSD research
and engineering in the Office of Strategic Technology Protection and Exploitation.
She is the project lead for the Cyber Resilient Weapon Systems Body of Knowledge,
which she has been leading since April of 2020.
From 2009 up until her current project, she worked for OUSD R&E
as a member of the software analysis team.
Her previous experience includes program protection lead at Missile Defense Agency
and computational social science projects at DARPA.
She is a retired military engineering officer and a graduate
of the U.S. Military Academy at West Point.
So, so, welcome, Ms. Angela.
Next, please.
Next is Ms. Madison Rudy.
She also provides support for resilient system policy, guidance,
and standards in the OUSD Research and Engineering Office
of Strategic Technology and Protection and Exploitation.
She's a lead analyst for the cyber resilient weapon systems body of knowledge.
She provides additional support to the JFAC, Joint Federated Assurance Center.
Her research area focuses on threat and risk assessments, database development,
data analysis for software assurance.
She's a graduate of Penn State University with a BS in security risk analysis,
focusing on information and cybersecurity.
Go, Penn State.
And lastly, next slide, we have Mr. Burhan Adam.
He is the Director for Resilient System Policy, Guidance and Standards in the OUSD Office
of Strategic Technology Protection and Exploitation.
He leads a secure cyber resilient engineering standards area
under the defense standardization program.
He is responsible for overseeing technology protection, technical information,
program protection, supply chain, cyber resilient weapon systems,
and system security engineering policy, guidance, acquisition regulations, standards,
education training, as well as engineering methods, tools, and techniques.
And now we'll hand it over to Mr. Burhan Adam to give his presentation.
>> Can you thank you, thank you Dr. Jacobs, thanks very much for those kind introductions.
As Dr. Jacobson said, within my area of responsibilities, among other things,
includes cyber resilient weapon systems engineering past products of collecting
and capturing and establishing best practices and developing support
and guidebooks associated with that of standards.
And so to share those things that we developed with the community,
with this [inaudible] community with the cyber center technology community,
and all the technical supporting teams, both of the industry side
and [inaudible] are stakeholders.
We needed to establish a means and way to have her technical repository, online repository,
I should say, to make that available, so that people can share information,
can communicate as needed, and able
to also facilitate some sort of a collaboration in that way.
So, this idea of the CRWS body of knowledge was sprung, and it's now in full operational
and as a team we have here today will walk you through that.
And I am very pleased that we have this opportunity to talk to you today.
And so thank you for your attendance.
And I think you will learn a few things from here.
And we expect people to leverage that among yourselves as well.
So, you know, please, please contact us if you need any help, and we'll walk you through that.
And through this brief, we'll give you enough information I think to get you started
and get you in the right direction.
Some of you may have a previous interest in it.
Some of you might have some more interest in it.
And might have even equities in it.
But we're here to help you out.
So, with that said, CRWS BoK is really an online repository capability to collect, like I said,
a warehouse, all technical information in the space,
in the area of cyber resilient worker systems engineering, from all sorts of people
in the industry, from our labs, within the DoD, even necessarily from,
you know, from a [inaudible] as well.
And also, you know, if we find something comes across, you know, from the other side
of the fellow government, we are interested in as well, because this is a problem
that affects a lot of people across, across the full spectrum or industry in government.
So, we established this [inaudible] to allow, again, government industry and academia
to share technical information in this space.
And it's a resource that will support our ability to decide and develop
and implement policy and strategy to design, build,
and deploy cyber resilient weapon systems.
So, we thank you again for this opportunity to introduce you to this online repository.
We'll give you insights into the capability and functionality
and walk you through its [inaudible] points.
So, I'm just kicking off the brief, to be honest, and setting up this stage for Angela
and Madison to walk you through it.
They will tag team in providing you the information today.
And Angela and Madison will be, you know, the introductions quickly,
so I don't need to add anything in introducing them, unless they wanted to say something more
about what they do, but I think you have enough information there,
how they have been doing this for the past 10 years.
And they have been really capable hands helping us out in putting this together.
So, with that, that's the agenda.
A quick diagram.
I will touch on the vision of this capability quickly.
And then from there, Madison will take over to walk you through the CONOPS of the capability
and how it operates, what are some responsibilities, and how we manage the creation
and the ability to maintain it and move and update us as necessary.
Angela then will take over from there, walk you through the structure and how the organization
and the functionalities of the portal.
And she will also share with you what we're doing
to move forward in terms of outreach like today.
And then hopefully we'll get some feedback from you as, you know, as potential users.
And we'll then after that we're happy to take any questions after we go through that.
So, next [inaudible] please.
There's a lot of words on this chart.
And really mission statement normally is shorter than that.
But anyways, you have here in a nutshell what the vision is.
And I'm not, you know, going to read the words.
But you get this.
In a nutshell, it's a digital, a digital repository of the CRWS body of knowledge
and information that the community is developing, that we are collecting, curating,
and storing and sharing among engineering and science and technology community,
including industry partners in academia.
Really the goal of the CRWS BoK is, is to reenact the repository.
And I'm repeating myself, but really I can't emphasize enough.
For learning about the secure cyber resilient engineering.
I mean, that is, you may ask why, what's that, what does it mean,
it's a whole lot of new concepts, ideas that we necessarily not new, but we haven't thought
about it, and we've got to make sure that our systems that we develop are operated
on a resilient as intended from any cyber.
And that is a huge area of research as we speak.
And it's a problem that affects across the board in the industry as well as us.
And we're working through that.
And we collected that information.
Dr. Jacobs, who is here, is in the middle of that from a training perspective.
So, we are in the midst of that.
So, this capability will help us out in terms of collecting that information
that the best practices, the things that are currently being discovered that works.
The methodologies, the tools, the information that supported that.
So, we are, you know, at the end of the day, we want to design and include a cyber resiliency
into the design and operations of the weapons systems.
And to do that, we have to collect, you know, what works, what doesn't work,
what part is it that we can establish the right policies, the right standards.
And getting that and doing the homework is important.
And collecting the technical information, it's important.
Working with industry, academia is important.
And this is so that we can train our people and help them out in terms
of putting together the things that they need to do [inaudible].
So, again, it's a resource for our community and the stakeholders.
And I will take any questions you may have before we started.
If not, we'll just move onto the brief with starting off with Madison.
>> All right, thank you, Burhan.
So, just to get us started, I'm going to go over a couple of the key features
that CRWS BoK is built upon that helps distinguish it from other bodies of knowledge
that we find to be extremely useful to the community.
First off is that the CRWS BoK is built off of highly,
high quality curated, publicly available resources.
And I'll get into this a bit later, just to further define what exactly our criteria is
for what resources go into the CRWS BoK.
But these are all available in a single web portal.
Instead of having the community going out and searching for valuable resources,
they're all available in one location.
I'll get into this as well later.
But the CRWS BoK is also regularly updated with authoritative,
highly specialized engineering knowledge resources.
Again, these are based off of certain criteria that the CRWS BoK team has established.
And we go through this process quarterly to make sure that resources are being added,
as well as ensuring that the resources we do have are up to speed
with the current community standards.
The CRWS BoK portal is also a powerful [inaudible] environment.
Angela will get into the features later.
But it's very user friendly, and allows for a lot of, a lot of community research
to be available, as well as annotations along with others.
And it's also a, like I mentioned, user friendly interface with opportunities
for direct feedback from registered users.
Next slide.
So, the CRWS BoK stakeholders currently are OUSD R&E, the Under Secretary
of Defense for Research & Engineering.
STP&E, resilient systems, as well as SAIC.
And as mentioned prior, our intended user base are those
in the secure cyber resilient engineering systems and adjacent communities.
So, this might include engineers, program managers, S&T managers, basically any system
that has a cyber component probably needs to be resilient, and we expect those community members
to find something of use on the CRWS BoK.
So, who's in charge of adding or removing content?
And this goes back to what I mentioned earlier about the curation process.
So, we have a group of, we have a review board consisting of content management stakeholders
that are representative members from government industry and academia, such as STP&E, CITAG,
NDIA, and SERC, that get help from the curation team to process
through nominated resources for inclusion in the CRWS BoK.
Next slide.
So, the general lifecycle for how resources get added to the CRWS BoK is
that any registered user can nominate a resource for inclusion within the CRWS BoK.
And these candidate resources will be packaged by the curation team
for then the review board's consideration.
So, all nominated resources will be put up for curation,
for review board's review, but not all will be included.
And there is a holding area that resources are placed
into so they won't immediately be available in CRWS BoK until they are reviewed.
The review board will adjudicate quarterly on whether resources meet all
of the acceptance criteria for inclusion in the repository.
And the curation team will then consolidate the findings, prepare the approved resources,
and move them to a CRWS BoK repository.
And by prepare the approved resources, this means tagging them appropriately
with proper metadata tags, and then finally relocating them
to the CRWS BoK from the holding area.
Next slide.
The acceptance criteria has been predetermined.
As I mentioned, none of the resources within CRWS BoK are classified,
so it's all publicly releasable material,
all approved for unrestricted public release, so nothing is sensitive.
Any restricted public material, so anything you had to [inaudible]
or with other associated exclusivity to a certain, certain sources, will have a title
and a link within CRWS BoK, but the resource itself will not be available.
Any foreign or sovereign owned material is not accepted for inclusion within the CRWS BoK.
Documents in draft, just because of the constantly changing nature, can be nominated,
but currently we only accept finalized drafts, or finalized versions of resources
to actually be uploaded to the CRWS BoK.
So, while we can review them when they're in draft, we don't want to add them to the CRWS BoK
until they are viewed as authoritative and a finalized version.
And finally we have a list of topics of interest that we have consolidated
that will be consulted for resource relevancy.
And this is available in the backup slides for any of those interested.
Next slide.
In order to maintain quality on the CRWS BoK,
because the field of cyber resilience is constantly changing, we want registered users
to be able to nominate new resources for consideration to be added to the CRWS BoK.
As I mentioned, there's also an ongoing verification
of resources for most current versions.
So, any type of updated version will be checked and added to the CRWS BoK.
So, if you come to the website, if you come to the portal,
you can guarantee that you are getting the most up to date version
of the resource available through, available to the public.
Registered users also have notification when new resources are published.
And Angela will get into this a bit later.
We also send out notification when resources are retired or rescinded or removed from CRWS BoK.
And we leverage algorithms and metrics to determine resource review schedules.
So, this might be if a resource has been available for a certain amount of years,
or if it's not frequently being accessed by users, if it has a poor user review rating,
we might put it up for consideration for removal.
And with that, I will hand it over to Angela to get into the features of the CRWS BoK.
>> Okay, so thank you, Madison for that.
Sorry for the little hiccup there.
So, I'm going to go ahead and cover the current features of CRWS BoK.
And most recently, we released Version 1.3 of CRWS BoK at the beginning of February.
And that introduced several new capabilities and improvements to CRWS BoK overall.
And I am going to include that in today's discussion.
So, as I mentioned, this slide is going to focus on just the current features,
including those newest releases in 1.3.
And I've broken it up into three categories here, those dealing with when you open
up the resources that you're looking at.
And just for clarification, when I say resources,
that refers to the actual documents that are in the repository.
And I'll use that term resources throughout.
So, when you open up a resource, some of the features that we have,
you can view it in we have what we call PDF viewer, so that you can view
and annotate the resource in the PDF version.
You can print, you can make it as a favorite, you can share that resource amongst others
within the community via e mail, SMS, text, a variety of ways you can share that as a link.
And that will get you directly into CRWS BoK to open up the resource.
You can actually view the resource details and have reference links to the Office
of Primary Responsibility, or OPR.
And the source, the original course document.
And, again, as Madison had mentioned, these are all publicly available documents, so you can,
we'll always have the source link listed alongside the actual resource file,
which is within the CRWS BoK repository.
And then we also have qualitative and quantitative ratings within CRWS BoK
for each of the documents or resources.
And then we have relationship mapping, and we have reference table views,
which I'll get into all of these in detail.
I'm just going to give you a summary here.
And in the general features, we have, as Madison had alluded to, we have notifications.
So, users, and, again, these are registered users, we have guest users,
and then we have registered users, and registered users can sign up for notifications
for whenever there's a new version that's uploaded into CRWS BoK.
Or, for example, when there's a saved search, whenever there's a new resource that is uploaded
that meets the criteria of a user's saved search.
And so all those notifications are, are enabled, and you can set the frequencies of those.
We have optional card views or list views.
And you'll understand a little bit more of that as I go into that in the next slides.
We have help boxes scattered throughout the site to help users understand or get more information
on various features within CRWS BoK.
We have accessibility features, and we have Section 508
on accessibility reviews done regularly on the site to ensure
that it's fully accessible to all users.
We have site maps to better enable navigation, e mail support so that you can always get back
to the curation or support team if there's any problem.
And the ever popular dark mode that was requested through,
we do a lot of frequent usability tests,
and dark mode is a highly requested feature that we did include.
So, we do a lot of regular usability testing, and we take those, that feedback very seriously
and incorporate those in a lot of the, the upgrades and new versions that we release.
And in the search features, you'll see that we have both guided search for those
that may not be familiar with a lot of the resilient terminology, or the field in general.
And then it helps them get a feel for where they need to go.
Then you have a very direct keyword search that you can search
and get right to where you need to go quickly.
You have a variety of filters, such as keyword filters, and additional filters that help narrow
in those searches once you get that.
You can, as I mentioned, save those searches
and have those update notifications sent to you as the user.
Again, these are for the registered users.
And you can actually do secondary searches within a document.
Again, this is tied back to the PDF viewer.
And you can have very defined filters.
So, there's a lot of capability that we have embedded and we are constantly looking
to improve those, again, based on a lot of the user feedback.
So, some of our plan features, and, again, this is tied based to our usability testing,
AI assisted relationship mapping.
We're constantly improving that feature.
And that has been very popular view that we have, and I'll cover that,
and continued enhancements to that relationships and reference both of those views.
Regular user interface improvements to make it easier and more satisfying experience for users
when they get to the CRWS BoK site.
And the ability to save annotations that a user may make to the popular documents.
The user has the ability to save those annotations so that when the user signs back
onto CRWS BoK, they can access those again.
And, again, this does not affect the integrity of the original documents.
This is only for the user's copy.
And then we have dynamic community metrics.
So, we're working, we're in the process of that right now, of getting those embedded
so that you can dynamically see all users when they log in will be able
to dynamically see what are the top 10 search terms, what are the top 10 resources
that are viewed by other users within the community, and provide,
be able to provide customized, serve up customized recommendations based
on if you're searching for this, you may be interested in that.
So, similar to Amazon or some other sites.
And then design patterns templates.
We're working on that ability as well.
So, these are some of the planned features.
And there's a lot more, but these are some of the ones we're working on right now.
So, I'll start with the landing page, which is what most users,
what you'll see when you first sign in to CRWS BoK, go back here, so when you first sign
in to CRWS BoK, and you can sign in as a guest user, or, which is you can be a registered user,
but it is not necessary to be a registered user.
The difference is is that when you are a registered user, you have access to some
of those notifications, some of those saved searches, and some of those other features
that we've discussed that require you to be a registered user.
But there is not a requirement.
You can still be a guest user and search and find and view these resources.
So, there's two ways to search, as we mentioned.
You can, one is the guided search, which is what you see here on these three main blocks.
And those are designed around the baseline framework of knowledge areas,
which basically represent the taxonomy of relevant cyber resilient
and systems engineering concepts from the ISO IEEE 1529.
Most engineers are familiar with that.
And so you see in the first two boxes, those represented through the area
to protect, and the technical process.
And the users select from those menu items there in those two boxes.
And once you make your selection, you'll see the results in the third box there.
So, in this case, there was mission and system function.
And then stakeholder requirements.
Those two were selected.
If you don't have a need to do that, you can just type in the keyword directly at the top,
in that top white box there, text box at the top of the window, and you can get directly to the,
whatever resource you're looking for.
Before we move on, I want to highlight, for those, there are other user areas,
other features, you can get to the profile settings in the far upper right you'll see,
for example, you'll see my sign in, [inaudible], with a little profile icon.
When you click on that, the drop down menu will show you a lot
of other settings that you can get to.
And that's where you will find the favorites, the saved searches,
and changing your password, for example.
Moving from right to left, you'll see this little half Sun shaded.
That's the dark mode, light mode that
The alarm bell icon.
And that's, again, for setting your notifications or new notifications.
That little plus icon, plus symbol there, is for your, changing your notifications.
Or I'm sorry, for adding, nominating a resource.
And this is where we get a lot of the community involvement to nominate a resource.
And this is where it goes through, as Madison described earlier, that nomination process.
And then again the typical, the home icon represented by the house.
Then you'll also see the news, which provides regularly updated rotates any news items.
And then key tips on the bottom box there on the right, different ways to search, for example,
or different highlighted tips that we'll regularly cipher through.
And then at the very bottom, you're going to see a, let's see if I'm not hiding this here,
it's cut off a little bit, but on the very bottom of the screen, on the footer,
you will always have the site information and help links.
And that's always available for the user when they're going throughout the site.
They'll be able to see that.
And they can find help boxes whenever you hover over any
of these boxes, you'll see a lot of that.
And you'll see in the upper right hand of the main window a help, help words there.
And that will also give you an ability to e mail the curation team or support team.
When you first sign on to CRWS BoK, and you can always turn this off and then go to it
through that profile when you go in that drop down menu, there's a, you can always get back
to the guided tutorial, but it will greet you the first time with this guided tutorial,
which will take you through all the features, and it will, here's just the first one,
and it will take you through all the key areas, just to let, and kind of walk you through some
of these features for the very first time.
What I'm showing you here is what we call the card view.
And the card view is the default view that you'll see.
And I have circled in the far, in the upper right corner,
you'll see list view circled in red.
And you have the option to change it if you would like to see more results shown in a more,
in a list view, you have the option to do that.
Right now, you're seeing the card view.
And what you're seeing is the results, the search results.
When you clicked either the guided search, or you entered in your direct keyword search
in that text box at the top, you will then be presented
with all your individual search results and your resources represented on each
of those cards that you see there.
Each of those cards will have some summary information.
So, you'll see just the most essential snapshot details.
The first that you'll see has the title, the domain, preview image.
You'll see the version information, user rating, and usability rating.
So, the user rating, which is at the, each of those words,
it's in the upper right hand corner, we call it the Lisa Simpson icon,
it reminds me of Lisa Simpson's hair, these are all silver.
They can either be silver, gold, or bronze.
And there's an algorithm.
If you hover over it, it will give you that information
and tell you what it actually represents.
But the usability rating is a quantitative decision support feature.
And it basically helps the user assess the value of each of those resources.
What we have for the initial algorithm has several factors that go into that rating,
such as domain type, the age of the document, and whether or not it's gone
through a formal peer review, for example.
And how long it is, the age, for example.
And that basically allows, these are all features that help the user quickly sort
through visually the value of each of those resources.
In the upper left, you'll see the various icons, and they're color coded to match.
We have authoritative government documents, which are laws or DoD issuances.
Then you have other government issuances,
which could be government white papers, or guide books, for example.
And then the third category is academic or industry documents or resources.
And so those are all color accordingly.
And you'll see those.
The green, for example, is an academic or industry document.
The purple, in the second item there, resource, you can see is a DoD issuance.
That's a government, authoritative government.
And then you'll see the beige color brown beige, which is in other government.
So, those are the domains that we call.
And then you'll see the other functional essential items.
You'll see a star rating at the bottom.
Those are user, the community users have the opportunity to evaluate the usefulness
of those resources to the ability to perform their tasks
and how useful they found that document.
There's the ability, as you see with the heart icon, for the user to favorite,
I'm using that as a verb, you can make the resource a favorite document,
you can select it to be notified of a, notification of any time it's updated.
You can download it, either print it or save it to your local directory.
And then you have a variety of that you can actually share the link.
And then you can actually look at the relationships tab.
And then you can also look at the quick abstract of the document.
So, on the left side, you have also the ability to filter.
And that's where you can refine your search and provide additional keyword filters.
Or apply any of those additional filters that you see below that on the left side.
And then in the middle of the screen, you'll see in dark purple save, or search terms.
Those are all the search terms.
And you can quickly, very quickly delete those if you want to refine that particular search.
And just click on the X and it removes that search term.
And it will dynamically, instantly update your search results.
Right above that deep purple, you'll see save search.
And that's where you can also save that search that you've now refined.
And you can save that, and then elect to be notified or not notified,
but you'll always have that save search for later use.
So, again, just quickly, this shows you how to save that search.
Again, go to that save search.
This shows you what that save search dialogue box will look like.
You can name it, provide a little description.
And then elect, if you want daily or weekly notifications to be sent to you.
And, again, this is for registered users.
And then you have what I'm showing you here is the list view that I mentioned earlier.
And it has similar information.
Does that work there?
So, this allows the ability to save the resource as a favorite.
And, again, this image, using the and here is the more detailed using the list view.
And selecting my favorite.
And very similarly, you can access that through the profile icon.
And then as I mentioned at the very beginning from that main page at the top,
those icons with the plus, the plus icon, that is how a user, and, again,
this is only for registered users, they would be able to nominate a resource.
And that's once they click on the nominate button icon,
they would be presented with a form to complete.
And you can see the information there.
There's some that they don't need to fill out all of it.
But that goes into, as Madison described, a holding repository.
And then the curation team reviews that,
packages it for the review board on a quarterly basis.
Once it's voted on, if it is approved, per the acceptance criteria, it then gets moved
over once it's vetted, validated, and metatagged,
it gets moved over into the open CRWS BoK repository.
But this is how the process is initiated from the user's perspective, perspective to nominate.
And we try to do that to get the user involvement,
to make sure that that repository is relevant to the, to the community at large.
And, again, this is going back to the PDF viewer.
So, when you double click on each of those cards, either from the card view
or the list view, those just show you the list view
and the card view showed you the essential information.
When you double click on each of those particular resource,
it will open up what we call the details view.
And from the details view, you then have four tabs.
You see in there viewer details relationships and references.
And the first of those is the viewer tab.
And the viewer tab allows the viewer to do a whole host of things to that, that resource.
And, again, this does not affect the original document in the repository.
It is only the user's, the registered user's local copy.
And you can print it, you can save it, share it, you can annotate, highlight, underline.
You can also do, as in this case, you can do a secondary search.
So, in this case, there was a document pulled up,
the cybersecurity test and evaluation guidebook.
And then a secondary search was done for PPP.
And then you can see in there the various instances of PPP
within that document, that resource are highlighted.
And if there is any question as to how or what types of annotations can be done,
you can always, again, using those help icons, or help dialogue boxes, open it up,
which I show here all the various editing, typical editing capabilities
that are available from that, from that PDF viewer.
And then again, the next tab over is what we call the details tab.
And that details tab gives you some more, as the name implies,
details pertaining to that particular resource.
